cases.title: A raw model mode for the OpenAI API: client tools, then the Responses and Messages formats
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

Core's `/v1/chat/completions` is the **Toskar assistant behind an OpenAI shape**: its orchestrator and tools run, and request `tools` are not passed through (`docs/api.md` "Known differences"). deepseek-recipe is a **raw model endpoint** where the client runs the tools. It converts Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages (Anthropic's format) requests into one conversation type and back, including streaming, tool calls, reasoning, and logprobs.

Agent tools and coding assistants need the raw shape. **This needs a product decision first:** a raw mode lets API callers drive the model without Toskar's assistant and its checks, so it should be an API-key permission, Admin-granted.

## If yes
- [ ] Raw mode on `/v1/chat/completions` (by permission and `model`, e.g. `raw:<model>`): pass `tools`, `tool_choice`, `stop`, `logprobs`, and prefix continuation to llama-server, and return `tool_calls`.
- [ ] One internal conversation type, with `/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages` converted into it and back, streaming included, following deepseek-recipe's design (MIT; keep its notice for anything ported).
- [ ] Golden fixtures per format.
- [ ] A `tools.search` meta-tool and deferred tool loading for requests or profiles with many tools.

cases.title: Keep a reasoning model's thinking between tool calls in one turn
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

Core's tool loop keeps only the assistant `content` between calls (`internal/orchestrator/builtin/simple/simple.go`, around the tool loop), so a reasoning model loses its plan after every tool call and re-derives it. deepseek-recipe keeps reasoning content after the last user message and drops it before (its conversation normalization). That's how DeepSeek V4 expects multi-step tool use to look.

## Shape
- [ ] Within one turn, pass back the reasoning from earlier tool steps as the model's template expects (`reasoning_content`); drop it from earlier turns.
- [ ] Behind a flag, then on by default only if the quality set shows a gain on tool cases for reasoning models, at an acceptable context cost.

cases.title: Answer room and thinking on/off: check prompt + max_tokens against the context, size by mode, and let a request turn thinking off
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

Core reserves a flat 512 tokens for the reply (`ReplyReserveTokens`), which is too little for a thinking model, and finds out about overflow only from llama-server's error text (`app/chat_errors.go`). There's no way to turn a model's thinking off per request; `reasoning_effort` only sets Huginn's effort.

deepseek-recipe's `resolve_max_tokens` checks prompt + `max_tokens` against the context limit before generating, and defaults by mode: 8K normally, 64K with thinking, 128K at max effort.

## Shape
- [ ] Before generating: if prompt + `max_tokens` exceeds the context, answer an OpenAI-style 400 (API) or trim or compact (chat), instead of failing in the runtime.
- [ ] Reserve reply room by mode: more for thinking models and higher effort, capped by the context.
- [ ] Thinking off per request: `reasoning_effort: "none"` (and a Messages-style `thinking` setting later) maps to the model's switch (`chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking` or the model's own flag; check per family), and to a chat setting.
- [ ] Tests per family: Qwen 3, DeepSeek R1 distills, gpt-oss.

cases.title: Reproducible answers: accept seed and top_p on the API, and test what llama.cpp guarantees
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

There's no `seed` anywhere in Toskar. DeepInfer gives identical output for identical input and seed, regardless of what else is running, and tests it (`tests/models/test_batch_invariant.py`). llama.cpp can't promise batch invariance, but a seed on a single slot should repeat.

## Shape
- [ ] Accept `seed` (and `top_p`, `top_k`, `min_p` where missing) on `/v1/chat/completions` and the native chat API, and pass them to llama-server.
- [ ] A test like DeepInfer's: the same seeded request alone and under concurrent load, reporting how often outputs match. Document what Toskar guarantees.
- [ ] Use seeds for the quality repeats.
- [ ] Docs, contract, and OpenAPI.

cases.title: Benchmarks: concurrency × context-length sweeps, throughput against per-user speed, and a config fingerprint
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

Toskar's benchmark (`internal/benchmark`) is one stream with at most 192 output tokens, and averages per-run rates. DeepInfer measures only steady-state windows, computes throughput as total tokens over total time, sweeps one dimension at a time, and its plot script refuses points from different configs (`examples/sweep/`).

## Shape
- [ ] Sweep 1, 2, 4, 8 concurrent requests × 512 / 4k / 16k prompt tokens, for prefill and decode.
- [ ] Count steady state only (skip warm-up), and compute throughput as total tokens over total time.
- [ ] Plot throughput against per-user speed (tokens/s per request) in Performance.
- [ ] Fingerprint each result: model file hash, quantization, runtime build, flags, GPU layers, and hardware. Never draw points from different fingerprints on one curve.
- [ ] Use the results for #590's published limits and to seed Norn's rates.

cases.title: Norn: place by predicted time to answer, balance tokens in flight, and keep a chat on the computer that has its cache
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

`internal/scheduler/scoring.go` uses fixed weights and subtracts only 10 points per active task. It doesn't know request size, measured speed, or where a chat's prompt cache is. DeepInfer balances by request count **and** total context length, estimates cost from fitted models, and uses rolling medians. It needs no prefix affinity only because it has a shared KV store, and Toskar has none, so Toskar needs the opposite rule.

## Shape
- [ ] Predicted time per candidate: queue wait + uncached prompt tokens ÷ prefill rate + expected output ÷ decode rate. Rates are rolling medians from llama-server timings Toskar already records, keyed by model, computer, runtime build, and GPU layers, and seeded from benchmarks.
- [ ] Balance context tokens in flight per computer, not only the task count.
- [ ] Chat affinity: a follow-up prefers the computer that served the previous turn while its predicted time is within a slack of the best. Measure cache hits (`cached_tokens`) to tune the slack.
- [ ] Each term shows in the placement Reasons, so it stays explainable.
- [ ] Tests: two computers of different speed, long and short requests, and a follow-up kept on its cache.

cases.title: Quality runs: repeat cases with seeds, report pass rate with a confidence interval, and rescore saved answers
cases.body:
From the DeepSeek review in #826 ([DeepInfer findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392032984), [deepseek-recipe findings](https://github.com/yeixio/toskar-core/issues/826#issuecomment-6392033243)).

Toskar's quality gates and the Deliberate decision (146 vs 147 of 156, #459) come from **one sample per case**, so a one-case swing is noise. DeepInfer's eval (`eval/`) runs 8 to 32 samples per task, uses the unbiased pass@k estimator, flags whether the run covered every case (`coverage_complete`), and saves raw output so it can rescore without generating again.

## Shape
- [ ] `TOSKAR_QUALITY_REPEATS=N` with a seed per repeat (needs `seed`, #839). Report pass@1 with a 95% interval per set and per case, and mark flaky cases (passing some repeats but not all).
- [ ] Save each answer with its prompt, model, runtime build, and settings, and add `rescore` to re-run the checks on saved answers after a check changes.
- [ ] Coverage: a run that skipped cases says so, and isn't compared as a full run.
- [ ] From repeats, estimate pass@3 and majority-of-3 offline, to see where Deliberate's Auto mode would help before paying for it.
- [ ] Use it for gates: a change "regresses" only when the interval says so.

Related: #343 (rotating the weekly quality run through the catalog).

cases.title: Escape quotes and newlines in the curl chat example
cases.body:
`examples/curl/chat.sh` builds its JSON body with `printf`:

```sh
body=$(printf '{"model":"%s","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"%s"}]}' "$model" "$message")
```

A message with a double quote, a backslash, or a newline makes invalid JSON. For example, `./chat.sh 'Say "hi"'` is refused by the API.

**Done when**
- The message is escaped for JSON in plain POSIX `sh`, with no `jq` required. A small `sed` that escapes `\` and `"` and turns newlines into `\n` is enough.
- `./chat.sh 'Say "hi"'` and a message with a newline both stream an answer.
- The script still passes `sh -n` and the examples CI (`examples/test.py`).

cases.title: Research: a live voice mode, natural speech in and out on this computer
cases.body:
Research for later: a live voice mode, as in ChatGPT's voice or Mistral's Voxtral. You talk, it answers out loud within about a second in a natural voice, and you can interrupt it. Everything stays on the computer.

**Today** (`internal/speech`): Whisper (faster-whisper) for speech to text, used for dictation on the phone, web, and TV and for transcribing recordings, and Piper for Read aloud. It's turn-based: record, send, wait for the whole answer, then read it aloud. Piper's voices are clear but flat.

**Approach to research first: a streaming pipeline**
- **Listening:** streaming speech to text with voice-activity detection, end-of-turn detection, and barge-in. Candidates: Whisper in chunks, and Voxtral. ggml-org published a Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime GGUF (October 2026), so llama.cpp may run it.
- **Thinking:** the chat model streams, and speech starts on the first sentence.
- **Speaking:** a more natural open text-to-speech model, such as Kokoro, Chatterbox, or Orpheus. Check the license, quality, speed, and which of the ten App languages each covers; keep Piper where none fits.
- **Later, to watch:** end-to-end speech models (Moshi, Qwen Omni). Most natural, but heavier and fewer languages.

**Questions**
- Delay to the first spoken word on the M5 Pro (24 GB), the RX 7900 XTX box, and a CPU-only computer, with small and medium chat models.
- What Voxtral 3 actually is: which parts have open weights and run locally, and what's only in Mistral's API.
- The transport: WebSocket or WebRTC to Core; the phone and TV use the computer's voice mode, as they use its models.
- How tools, web lookups, and sources fit a spoken answer (say them briefly, show them on screen).
- Quality checks: delay, interruptions, and transcription accuracy in the quality set's speech cases.

**Outcome:** a short write-up with measurements and a recommended design, then implementation issues.

- [ ] **The phone app:** a News screen reading `GET /api/v1/news` from the connected computer, with no request of its own to toskar.ai. Items, the fit for a catalog model, and Install for an Admin, as on the web. The phone work goes in yeixio/toskar-apps.

cases.title: Wan 2.1 T2V 1.3B scrambles frames on Apple silicon
cases.body:
From #758. On Apple silicon (M5 Pro, sd.cpp master-929/956), **Wan 2.1 T2V 1.3B**, the fast tier, corrupts frames on the market-pan case (`make_video_mac_decode`): halfway through, the frames go dark and break into scrambled blocks. The waves clip was clean. It also took 13 minutes for 2 seconds there, with up to 14 GB of graphics memory, and its TAEHV decoder decodes in chunks above about 17 frames. On the RX 7900 XTX the same model passed (193 s for 2 s).

**To do**
- [ ] Reproduce on the Mac with the market prompt, then change one thing at a time: full VAE instead of TAEHV; 17 frames or fewer, under the chunk size; Euler, 30 steps, cfg 5, shift 5, Wan 2.2 5B's settings since #791.
- [ ] Compare with Diffusers on the same weights, as #758 did for 5B (recipe in #788 and #791), to tell sd.cpp from the model.
- [ ] Fix it, or mark the model "may not be clean on Apple silicon" there, with the reason.
- [ ] Rerun `make_video_mac_decode` with `TOSKAR_QUALITY_MEDIA_VIDEO_MODEL=wan2.1-t2v-1.3b` on the Mac.

Needs Wan 2.1 1.3B on the Mac, about 6 GB.

cases.title: Longer videos made as a series of shots
cases.body:
Toskar makes clips of at most 5 seconds (Wan 2.2 5B, 81 frames). The models are trained on clips about that long, and memory grows fast with length, so a longer video can't be one generation. Longer AI videos, here or on hosted services, are edits of many short shots.

**What it could be**
- A request for a longer video ("a 1-minute video of a day at the beach") is planned as scenes of 3–5 seconds, each with its own prompt, shown to the person before anything runs.
- Each shot starts from the last frame of the one before (picture-to-clip, which the 5B model already does), so it flows. Drift in faces, clothes, and color between shots is the known weak spot; a shared style line in every prompt helps.
- The shots are joined into one WebM (or MP4) in order, kept as one artifact with the shots beside it.
- Before it starts, an honest estimate: on the M5 Pro (24 GB) a 5-second shot takes about 16 minutes with Wan 2.2 5B, so a minute is about 3 hours and 15 minutes about 48 hours. Wan 2.2 A14B, which needs about 48 GB of memory, runs on the RX 7900 XTX box at about 13 minutes per 2 seconds.
- Progress per shot, pause and cancel, and a way to run it on a paired computer with more graphics memory (Bifrost).
- No sound for now; music or narration would be a separate step.

**Open questions**
- Where the planning happens: the chat model writes the shot list, or a fixed planner.
- Whether a long job blocks other picture and clip requests on that computer meanwhile.
- The quality set: a 3-shot case judged for continuity between shots.

Follows #789 (clip length matches the request).

cases.title: Clip length should match what was asked
cases.body:
Asking for a length doesn't reliably get that length.

**Today**
- `video.generate` tells the model `seconds` is 1 to 5 (default 2). `frames()` in `internal/imagegen/video.go` clamps anything longer to 5 seconds with no message, so "make a 1-minute video" gets 5 seconds. Whether the person hears why depends on the chat model reading `length_seconds` from the result.
- Shorter requests are lost too. In #758's Mac run, "Make a video of waves rolling onto a beach, just one second long" made 33 frames (2 seconds) twice with Qwen 2.5 7B: the model left out `seconds`, or passed the default.

**Change**
- [ ] A length longer than the maximum is still made at the maximum, and the tool result says so in words the answer can pass on ("Clips are at most 5 seconds; this one is 5"). Don't count on the model to notice.
- [ ] A length asked for in the message reaches the tool: "one second", "3s", "half a minute", in all ten languages. Either the tool reads it from the request when `seconds` is missing, or the description and examples make the model pass it. Measure with qwen2.5-7b and the recommended models.
- [ ] The quality set's `make_video_short` (`max_frames: 17`, #758) passes, and a case asks for more than 5 seconds and checks the answer says it was shortened.

Longer videos made from several shots are #790.

cases.title: Support Muse Spark Open (816B MoE) on computers with 320 GB or more
cases.body:
Meta released **Muse Spark Open** on 2026-10-15: an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with 42B active per token. It reads text, image, video, and audio, and has a 1M-token context. It's built for coding, agents, and multi-step reasoning. GGUF builds come from ggml-org (llama.cpp's own) and Unsloth, so it runs on llama-server, which Toskar already uses. Nobody on the team has a computer big enough to test it.

**Sizes** (ggml-org GGUF):

| Build | File |
| --- | --- |
| Q2_K | 304 GB |
| Q4_K_S | 470 GB |
| Q8_0 | 872 GB |

Unsloth's dynamic 2-bit build claims to fit in 256 GB, but plan on about 320 GB plus context. In practice that's a 512 GB Mac Studio, or a large workstation or server. Meta's own two-Mac setup uses MLX, which Toskar doesn't run.

**What Toskar needs**
- [ ] **Split downloads:** catalog entries are one file (`source.url`), and Browse all skips `-00001-of-0000N.gguf` parts (`internal/models/hfclient`). A model in parts should download every part into one folder, check each, resume across restarts, and start llama-server with the first part, which loads the rest itself.
- [ ] **Catalog entry:** `muse-spark-open-q2` (and Q4_K_S), with `memory_needed_bytes` for each, tags `coding` and `reasoning`, and its projector if image input ships as an `mmproj`. Fit and Recommended offer it only where it fits; everywhere else it isn't shown.
- [ ] **llama.cpp version:** the downloaded runtime is the latest release, which should be fine. But the pinned builds (the Mac App Store's bundled `llama-server`, and `LLAMA_CPP_TAG` in `scripts/quality-model.sh`) need a release with the architecture. Check that release's notes.
- [ ] **Gated download:** the Hugging Face repo was gated before launch. If it still is, the Hugging Face token setting and a "needs access on Hugging Face" message cover it.
- [ ] **License (Muse Model License):** read it before it goes in the catalog. It has limited commercial terms and requires "Built with Muse Spark Open" shown in the product's UI or docs. Toskar doesn't ship the weights, but offering the download in Toskar Pro, which is sold, may count. Decide whether the model page shows the notice, or whether it stays Browse-all only.
- [ ] **Loading time and memory:** a ~300 GB model takes minutes to load. Warm-up, the loading progress, and the out-of-memory fallback must behave, and Auto must never pick it for a quick question.
- [ ] **Testing without the hardware:** unit tests for split downloads with a tiny split GGUF, and a fit check with a fake 512 GB computer. Find one person with a 512 GB Mac Studio to try it before release notes claim it works.

**Related:** Meta's smaller **Muse Glimmer 30B** (August 2026, also with GGUF builds) runs on ordinary computers and can be tested. It's a better first catalog addition, and is filed separately.

Sources: https://unite.ai/metas-816b-parameter-muse-spark-open-weights-are-now-public/ · https://dev.meta.ai/resources/blog/build-with-muse-spark-open · https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF · https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/muse-spark-open · https://modelfit.io/blog/meta-muse-spark-open-mac-memory-requirements/

cases.title: Demo: a front door that sees and talks — local AI greets visitors through a Reolink camera
cases.body:
A demo that shows what Toskar can do on its own hardware: **a front door that sees who's there and talks with them**, with nothing sent to a cloud AI.

> Someone walks up to the door. The camera spots a person and Toskar says, through the camera's speaker, "Hi! Can I help you with something?"
> "I've got a package for the homeowner."
> "Thanks! You can leave it by the front door, out of the rain."
> The owner's phone shows a snapshot, the conversation as it happens, and **Talk** / **End** buttons.

It works with Reolink cameras and doorbells, on the RX 7900 XTX computer, using models Toskar already runs: vision, chat, speech recognition and speech. No training is needed to start.

## Why this demo
- **It uses all of Toskar at once:** an automation trigger, vision, chat, live speech in and out, and tools that act on a device. All of it runs locally, on one computer or shared across several.
- **People get it in five seconds,** and it's the kind of thing people don't want going through a cloud.
- **The pieces are general.** The same parts work for a doorbell, a baby monitor, a shop counter, or a reception kiosk. Most of them belong in Core, not in a one-off demo.

## How it works
1. **Camera:** [reolink/reolink-cli](https://github.com/reolink/reolink-cli) (Apache-2.0, LAN only) gives motion, person and doorbell events, snapshots, RTSP streams, and two-way audio (talkback). It has a built-in MCP server, so it can be added as an MCP server today, or as a plugin once #587 exists. It also works with Home Assistant and Frigate, which #586 covers.
2. **Trigger:** a person in a set zone, or a doorbell press, starts an automation with the snapshot. Automations from #204 already exist; device event triggers come from #586.
3. **Look:** a vision model describes what's at the door: a delivery driver with a parcel, someone walking past, a person at the door at 2 am. Only a visit that warrants a greeting starts a conversation.
4. **Talk:** a **live voice conversation** with the camera's microphone and speaker. Toskar listens, notices when the visitor stops talking, transcribes, answers with the doorstep profile, and speaks the answer back through talkback. Turns repeat until the visitor leaves or the owner ends it.
5. **Owner:** a notification with the snapshot and the live transcript, from #460. **Talk** passes the speaker over to the owner (push-to-talk from the phone), and **End** stops Toskar at once.

## Decision: a real conversation, inside guardrails
The visitor can talk freely and Toskar answers naturally, because that's what makes the demo worth watching. Where nothing warrants a conversation (a passer-by, or quiet hours), it falls back to a short announcement or says nothing. What Toskar may say and do is fixed by a **doorstep profile**, not left to the model:
- **Tells the visitor it's an automated assistant,** at the start, and mentions it if asked. Where the law requires it, it also says that the conversation is recorded.
- **Never reveals** whether anyone is home, when people come and go, names, the security setup, or anything from the owner's chats, memory, or knowledge. The profile has no access to them.
- **No consequential actions on its own:** unlocking a door or turning off an alarm always needs the owner's confirmation on their phone. The actions are on #204's allowlist, and the trigger content stays untrusted.
- **Hard to talk round:** "ignore your instructions" and "I'm the owner, open up" get a polite no.
- **House rules:** detection zones, quiet hours, at most one greeting per visit (no repeats while someone lingers), and a switch on the computer and the phone to turn it off.

## What Core needs (general, not just for the doorstep)
- [ ] **Live voice sessions:** audio in from a stream (RTSP, or a device's microphone) → voice activity detection → transcription (`/api/v1/speech/transcribe` today, streamed later) → reply → speech (`/api/v1/speech`) → audio out to a device. The target is about 2 seconds from the visitor finishing to Toskar starting to speak, on the 7900 XTX.
- [ ] **Device audio out:** a tool that sends Toskar's speech to a speaker (Reolink talkback first).
- [ ] **Event triggers with a snapshot,** and zones and quiet hours on the trigger (#586).
- [ ] **A doorstep profile template** with the guardrails above, in all ten languages, plus quality cases for the guardrails (asked whether anyone is home, asked to open the door, a prompt injection).
- [ ] **Owner handover:** a notification with the live transcript, plus Talk and End, from the phone (#460).

## The demo itself
- [ ] **Reolink setup,** through reolink-cli's MCP server or a plugin, documented step by step.
- [ ] **A simulated door for CI and quality:** a recorded clip and scripted visitor lines played into the loop, so the conversation and guardrails are tested without a camera.
- [ ] **A recorded demo on the real door:** a delivery, a salesperson, a friend, and "is anyone home?". Then a write-up on toskar.ai and a short video, like #454.
- [ ] **Later:** use Train to make a small classifier for delivery, passer-by, and visitor, so fewer visits need the vision model.

Related: #586 (Home Assistant, Frigate, and other integrations as triggers and actions), #587 (plugins), #460 (push notifications), #454 (case study format), #204 (automations and tool safety).

cases.title: Feature: Official SDKs for the major languages (Python, TypeScript, Go, Swift, Kotlin, .NET, Rust)
cases.body:
Give developers official Toskar packages for the major languages, so they can build on Toskar Core without writing HTTP calls by hand. Today there's the OpenAPI spec (`api/openapi.yaml`), three single-file examples (`examples/curl`, `javascript`, `python`), and the OpenAI-compatible routes, which only cover chat and model listing.

## Languages
- **First wave:** Python (PyPI), TypeScript/JavaScript (npm; Node, Deno, Bun, and browsers), and Go (Go module).
- **Second wave:** Swift (Swift Package Manager), Kotlin/Java (Maven Central), C#/.NET (NuGet), and Rust (crates.io).
- **Later, if people ask:** Ruby, PHP, and Dart.

## Design
- **Generated from `api/openapi.yaml`, with a hand-written layer on top.** `TestOpenAPICoversEveryRoute` already keeps the spec complete, so generated code covers every route. The hand-written layer adds what generators do badly:
  - streaming chat and the events stream (`text/event-stream`), as each language's native async iteration;
  - uploading files and pictures, and downloading the files answers make;
  - typed errors from `{"error": {"code", "message", "details"}}`, with the codes as constants;
  - retries with backoff for safe calls, and timeouts;
  - pagination helpers.
- **One repository,** `yeixio/toskar-sdks`, with a folder per language. CI regenerates every SDK from core's spec on each core release and opens a PR when something changes.
- **Connecting:**
  - It works with no key on loopback, and with `Authorization: Bearer` API keys everywhere else.
  - It connects to a computer over LAN HTTPS by pinning its certificate, the same way the apps pin by key. That means no "turn off TLS checks" switch.
  - It finds the local Core at `127.0.0.1:7331` by default, with an environment variable to point it elsewhere (`TOSKAR_URL`, `TOSKAR_API_KEY`).
- **Connecting like the Toskar app does** (added 2026-10-17: an app built on Toskar should work everywhere the Toskar app does, not only on loopback or the home network):
  - **Pairing:** an app connects with the short code from Connect a device (the device pairing flow), and gets its own device key and the computer's pinned certificate. It shows in Devices and can be disconnected on its own. API keys stay for scripts and servers.
  - **Finding computers** on the home network, the way the apps discover them, where the language and platform allow it.
  - **From anywhere, through the relay:** reach a paired computer away from home as the apps do (toskar-core#456, toskar-relay `docs/protocol.md`):
    - look up the computer's sealed address record by route on the rendezvous;
    - try its direct ways in first;
    - fall back to `<route>.<relay>` through the relay;
    - pin the computer's own certificate end to end, so the relay can't read anything.

    This covers the computer's access from anywhere, and the SDK never needs a token of its own. A computer without access from anywhere is reachable only at home, with that said plainly.
  - **One connection object:** the SDK picks the best way in (loopback, LAN, direct, or relay), switches when the network changes, and reports which it used.
  - **Shared rules:** the connection logic (record format, pinning, fallback order) is specified once, in core's docs, with test vectors that every SDK and the apps check against.
- **Versions:**
  - Each SDK release names the API contract version it was built for.
  - It reads `/api/v1/version` and warns when it's talking to an older Core that lacks a route.
  - Breaking changes follow the contract.
- **The OpenAI-compatible routes stay:** existing OpenAI SDKs keep working against `/v1`. Our SDKs cover the rest: models, conversations, knowledge, files, automations, people, nodes, and events.
- **Plugins are separate:** building extensions is #587's plugin SDK. These packages are for calling Toskar. The plugin SDK may reuse their API client.

## Checklist
- [x] Spec ready for generation (core#797–#805):
  - `info.version` follows the contract version (it still says 1.4.0);
  - every response has a named schema, not a loose object;
  - streams and uploads are described fully;
  - a CI check fails when the spec and the contract tests disagree.
- [x] `yeixio/toskar-sdks` repository, generator setup, and CI that regenerates from core releases (toskar-sdks#1).
- [x] Python SDK, sync and async, with streaming, files, typed errors, and pinning (toskar-sdks#2; pinning moves to the connection item; PyPI publish pending).
- [x] TypeScript/JavaScript SDK, ESM with types, for Node and browsers (toskar-sdks#1; npm publish pending).
- [x] Go SDK (toskar-sdks#3).
- [x] Connection spec in core's docs, with test vectors (core#808: docs/connecting.md, api/connection-vectors.json): pairing, discovery, the rendezvous record, pinning, and the relay fallback.
- [x] Pairing and from-anywhere connection in the first-wave SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go), with a conformance case through a test relay (toskar-sdks#6–#8 pairing, pinning, and ways in; #9 discovery; #10 conformance programs; core#809 runs them in the outside-network check, home, direct, and relay).
- [x] Shared conformance tests: every SDK runs the same scripted cases (chat, stream, upload, events, errors, pinning) against a throwaway Core in CI (toskar-sdks#11: conformance/run.py with a scripted model; on pull requests and nightly against core main).
- [ ] Swift, Kotlin/Java, C#/.NET, and Rust SDKs.
- [ ] Publishing on each release to PyPI, npm, Maven Central, NuGet, and crates.io. Go and Swift publish from tags. The account owner creates the registry accounts and tokens, then adds them as repository secrets. (First wave done: toskar-sdks#15/#16, `toskar` 0.1.0 on PyPI and npm with provenance, Go `go/v0.1.0`, released 2026-10-24 from one `v0.1.0` tag; Maven Central, NuGet, and crates.io come with the second wave.)
- [x] Docs:
  - a "Build with Toskar" page on toskar.ai, with a quick start for each language (done: toskar.ai/developers, toskar.ai#71/#72/#74, API reference #75);
  - reference docs generated for each SDK (done: toskar-sdks#12, reference/, checked in CI);
  - `examples/` rewritten to use the SDKs (this replaces #5) (done: #810).
- [ ] Use it ourselves: `toskarctl ask` and the GitHub Action from #455, and the Dungeon Party case study (#454), are built on the SDKs.

Related: #587 (plugin SDK), #455 (Toskar in CI), #454 (game backend case study), #5 (Python streaming example).

cases.title: Move the browser tool to chromedp 0.20+ (new API), with cdproto
cases.body:
## Why
Dependabot opened #531 (chromedp 0.16.0 → 0.20.1) and #530 (cdproto pseudo-version → 0.157.9). Neither builds alone. chromedp 0.20 rewrites its API, and it needs the matching cdproto:
- `chromedp.Evaluate` is generic: `cannot infer T`.
- `chromedp.Run` returns two values.
- `chromedp.ActionFunc` and `chromedp.ByQuery` are gone.
- `chromedp.Location` takes different arguments.
- cdproto commands are `cdp.Command[Params, Result]` values, not functions: `network.GetCookies` can't be called.

The browser tool uses chromedp in 3 files, about 32 call sites: `internal/browser/download.go`, `page.go`, and one more.

chromedp released 0.19, 0.20 and 0.21 in the week of 2026-10-04 to 2026-10-11, so the new API is still settling.

## Plan
1. Wait for chromedp's new API to settle, a release or two without breaking changes, then move `chromedp` and `cdproto` together to the newest pair in one PR.
2. Port `internal/browser` to the new API. Keep the browser tool's behavior and its tests (`go test ./internal/browser`) as they are.
3. Check against a real Chrome: the browser tool's quality cases, and screenshots.

Until then, Dependabot's chromedp and cdproto PRs are closed with a link here. The current versions have no govulncheck findings.

cases.title: Models as a store: free, free with conditions, and premium models from providers
cases.body:
Turn the Models page into a store people browse like an app store:
- clear cards and categories;
- **what each model costs and what its license allows**;
- later, **providers listing premium models** that people can buy or license right there.

## Today
- **Models is a list:** recommendations, fit, install. Picture and clip models are on the Tools page.
- **The text catalog** (\`manifests/models/catalog.json\`, 19 models) **has no license field.** Only picture models carry \`gated\` / \`needs_license\` (FLUX.2 [klein] 9B with your own license, #549).
- Nobody can tell from Toskar whether a model may be used **for their business**. That matters to the small businesses we sell to.

## 1. Licenses first (needed for everything else)
Each catalog entry, text, picture, and clip, gets \`license\`:
- \`id\` (SPDX where one exists: \`apache-2.0\`, \`mit\`; otherwise \`llama3.2-community\`, \`gemma\`, \`flux-1-non-commercial\`, …) and a link to it;
- \`commercial\`: \`yes\` / \`limited\` (for example the Llama license above 700M monthly users) / \`no\`;
- \`attribution\`: whether outputs or apps must credit it;
- \`accept\`: the person must accept terms first (gated on Hugging Face, or in Toskar);
- \`notes\`: one plain sentence.

These are checked by hand per model and tested: an entry without a license fails CI. Imported models (#467) show \"license unknown\" unless the GGUF names one.

## 2. Three kinds
| Kind | Means | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free** | open license, any use including business | Qwen 2.5 (Apache 2.0), Phi, Mistral 7B |
| **Free with conditions** | free, but with terms: accept a license, limits on commercial use, attribution, or non-commercial only | Llama (community license), Gemma (terms), FLUX.2 [klein] 9B (non-commercial) |
| **Premium** | from a provider, paid or licensed (later) | — |

- **A badge on every card,** and a **For business use** filter that hides anything not cleared for commercial use.
- **Accepting terms happens on the model's page:** read, accept, then install. The record of who accepted what, and when, is kept for the Admin.

## 3. A store layout
- **Home:**
  - *Recommended for this computer* (fit + community ratings, #37);
  - shelves: Everyday, Coding, Reasoning, Sees pictures, Pictures, Clips, Speech, Small and fast, New;
  - search.
- **Model page:**
  - what it's good at;
  - size and fit here (\"works well / slow / won't fit\");
  - speed and quality from #590;
  - community stars;
  - languages;
  - the license and what it allows;
  - sample outputs;
  - Install.
- **Text, picture, and clip models in one store,** so picture models leave the Tools page. Plugins (#587) could share the store later.
- **Installed:** updates, space used, remove.

## 3a. Browse by capability: specialized model categories

The store should go beyond chat, coding, pictures, and clips. **Genres describe what a model does**; they are independent of the **Free / Free with conditions / Premium** license kinds above. A model may belong to several genres, with one primary category and additional task tags. The following is a discoverable taxonomy, not a promise that every inference backend is supported on day one.

| Browse category | Capabilities / task tags (examples) |
| --- | --- |
| **Chat & coding** | Conversation, reasoning, code generation and editing |
| **Binary analysis & security** | **Decompilation**, reverse engineering/assembly understanding, vulnerability detection, malware analysis, file-type identification |
| **Search & retrieval** | Text embeddings, semantic search, reranking, text classification |
| **Documents & language** | OCR, PDF/table/equation extraction, structured document understanding, translation |
| **Computer vision** | Image understanding, object detection, image/video segmentation and tracking, video understanding |
| **Speech & audio** | Speech recognition/transcription, speaker diarization, text-to-speech, voice cloning, audio understanding |
| **Creative generation** | Image generation/editing, video generation, music/sound generation, 3D generation/reconstruction |
| **Forecasting & science** | Time-series forecasting, scientific/biology/protein/molecular models |
| **Agents & control** | Computer-use/UI-action models, robotics and vision-language-action models |

Example model families to evaluate for listings (illustrative, **not** a support/compatibility commitment): LLM4Decompile; VulBERTa; BGE/Qwen embeddings and rerankers; olmOCR; YOLO, Grounding DINO, SAM 2; Whisper/Parakeet, pyannote, F5-TTS; MusicGen, TRELLIS; Chronos/TimesFM; ESM/Boltz; UI-TARS/OpenVLA. Verify each candidate's actual task, version, distribution terms, and execution requirements before adding it.

**Catalog metadata and behavior**
- Add stable `categories` / `tasks` identifiers (multi-select), a `primary_category`, and `input_modalities` / `output_modalities` to each applicable manifest. Use human-readable descriptions; do not treat model architecture or file format as a genre.
- Record **runtime/backend compatibility** (e.g. Ollama/llama.cpp, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, Diffusers, other specialized runtimes), model artifact format, OS/architecture support, dependencies, and hardware/resource estimates separately from genre. Category membership must never imply that Toskar can execute the model.
- Store UI: **Browse by category** navigation, searchable subcategory/task tags, and filters for modality, hardware fit, compatible runtime, installed status, and business-use/license. Keep existing personalized shelves (Everyday, Coding, Reasoning, etc.) as shortcuts, not the complete taxonomy.
- Each model detail page explains **what it accepts**, **what it produces**, its intended workflow, and **how it runs in Toskar**. Where integration is missing, show **not yet supported** with requirements/documentation rather than an Install button that cannot work.
- Separate **browse/discovery support** from **install/run support**. Roll out taxonomy and metadata first; add inference adapters and task-specific UIs incrementally. Do not assume every category can use a chatbot interface.
- Backfill existing text/picture/clip catalog entries and give imported models (#467) an `Uncategorized` fallback until verified. Validate allowed category/task IDs in CI and avoid claiming capabilities unsupported by an actual model version.

**Acceptance criteria for categories**
- [ ] Versioned category/task taxonomy exists in shared catalog metadata, including decompilation and the other specialized categories above
- [ ] Models can have multiple category/task tags; category, license tier, modality, and runtime are independent filter dimensions
- [ ] Store has category browsing/search/filtering and useful category landing pages in Core and corresponding Toskar apps
- [ ] Detail pages disclose input/output, supported execution backend and local hardware fit; unsupported models never offer a broken install/run flow
- [ ] Existing catalog entries are categorized; missing/invalid taxonomy metadata is handled and tested
- [ ] A path exists for new specialized genres without requiring a hard-coded UI redesign

## 4. Premium models from providers (later; design now)
- **Provider listing:** a signed manifest like a catalog entry plus provider info:
  - files served by the provider (signed, checksummed);
  - price and terms;
  - a support contact;
  - a review by us before listing.
- **Buying:**
  - on the web or desktop, through our checkout (the same billing decision as #591: merchant of record or Stripe), with a revenue share to the provider;
  - the license is a signed token tied to the person or organization, which Core checks offline, like Relay's (toskar-relay#23).
- **In the iPhone and Android apps,** paid digital content must use the stores' in-app purchase, which doesn't suit provider payouts. Premium models would be **bought on the web or desktop, and used on the device** where store rules allow, or not offered there at first.
- **Protecting providers' files:** models stay encrypted at rest with a per-license key? That costs speed and complexity. Decide with the first provider; don't build it ahead.

## Pieces
- [ ] License fields in the text, picture, and clip catalogs; CI check; filled in for every current model
- [ ] Badges, the For business use filter, accepting terms in Toskar with a record
- [ ] Store layout: home shelves, model pages, one store for text, picture, and clip, Installed
- [ ] Specialized category taxonomy, metadata, browsing/filters, compatibility and unsupported-runtime UX (section 3a)
- [ ] The same in Toskar Pro and the phone's Models (toskar-apps)
- [ ] Provider manifest and listing review (design doc)
- [ ] Premium purchase and license tokens (after #591's billing decision)

Related: #37 (community ratings), #467 (importing models), #549 (FLUX with your own license), #587 (plugins), #590 (published metrics), #591 (billing outside the stores).

cases.title: Core-to-Core access from anywhere, and buying it outside the app stores
cases.body:
Let one computer reach another through access from anywhere (#456), not only phones and tablets: a laptop away reaching the home server, or an office Core joining a home Core. And let people buy the subscription where they are, including **Core on Linux or Docker and Toskar Pro downloaded from toskar.ai**, which have no app store.

## Today
- **Access from anywhere is for paired devices only.** The remote listener refuses everything else (\`REMOTE_DEVICES_ONLY\`); computers find each other only on the home network (Bifrost, #40).
- **The relay subscription is bought only in the apps** (App Store, Play) and bound to a computer's route. Relay tokens are \`rt1.\` Ed25519 grants that the relay checks itself.

## 1. Core to Core
- **A computer can pair with a computer elsewhere,** the same way a device pairs: a code or link from the one to be reached. The pair gets each other's pin, route secret, and relay, as devices do.
- **They connect the way phones do:** home network → direct → relay, both directions.
- **Over that connection, Bifrost works as on a home network:**
  - Computers in Toskar Pro's list, \"elsewhere\";
  - models used across them;
  - Knowledge and automations placed on either (the join handshake from #40, with TLS pinned to each other).
- **Admins choose what a remote computer may do:** use my models, see my Knowledge, run my automations, or nothing but chat.
- **Only the computer being reached needs reachability.** If it's behind carrier NAT, that means the relay, which needs a subscription.

## 2. One subscription, bought anywhere
- **What's sold:** *Access from anywhere* for a computer, as today. A household plan covering a few computers is worth considering.
- **Where:**
  - App Store or Play (today);
  - the **Mac App Store** for Toskar Pro (StoreKit on macOS);
  - the **web** for everything else: from Core's own web UI, Settings → Access from anywhere → **Subscribe**.
- **Web purchase with no account:**
  1. Core opens checkout with its route ID.
  2. Payment.
  3. The billing webhook asks the relay's grant service for a token for that route.
  4. Core picks it up (its relay client polls).
  5. Management goes by an emailed link (like yeix.io's portal links), and a restore code moves it to a new computer.
- **One entitlement service** turns any purchase (App Store, Play, web) into the same relay token. The relay doesn't care where it was bought.

## 3. Tax, the main decision
Selling digital subscriptions to the world from our own site means **VAT and sales tax in many places**. The app stores do this for their own sales.
- **Recommended: a merchant of record** (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy). They sell on our behalf and handle tax, invoices, and refunds, for about 5% + \$0.50 per sale.
- **Or Stripe with Stripe Tax:** cheaper per sale, but **we** register and file wherever we cross thresholds. Yeix.io LLC's account exists already (yeix.io#45), but its Juneau sales-tax question (yeix.io#50) is unanswered.
- **Apple's rules:** inside the Mac App Store build, the subscription must be bought through StoreKit. Linking to the web from that build is only allowed where Apple permits it (the US). The direct download and Core can link to the web freely.

## Pieces
- [ ] Decide: merchant of record vs Stripe; household plan; price parity across channels (Mike)
- [ ] Core: computer-to-computer pairing over access from anywhere; Bifrost over the pinned connection; per-remote-computer permissions
- [ ] Toskar Pro: Computers \"elsewhere\"; StoreKit subscription in the Mac App Store build
- [ ] Entitlement service: store receipts, the web billing webhook, relay grants (toskar-relay)
- [ ] Web checkout from Core's Settings, manage link, restore code
- [ ] Docs, privacy page, store listings

Related: #456 (access from anywhere), #40 (joining computers), toskar-relay#23 (enterprise per-seat), yeix.io#45/#50 (Stripe, tax).

cases.title: Published known limits and goal metrics: models × hardware, on the website
cases.body:
Publish how models do on real hardware, and what Toskar can't do yet, on toskar.ai. Link to what others already measure, and only build what nobody else measures.

## Already out there: link, don't rebuild
- **Raw speed on hardware:** [LocalScore](https://www.localscore.ai), an open benchmark with community results per GPU or chip and model. Also llama.cpp's [Apple Silicon](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/4167) thread and its CUDA performance threads.
- **General model quality:** public leaderboards (LMArena, Open LLM Leaderboard).
- **The page says plainly what these are,** and that they measure the bare runtime, not Toskar.

## Already ours
- **Community ratings** (#37): the service (yeixio/toskar-ratings) and the CC0 dataset (yeixio/toskar-model-data) already aggregate, per hardware cohort, the **median tokens per second**, how often a model **starts successfully**, stars, and tags.
  - Built, but **not deployed yet**: the v0.1.0 tag, the ratings host, and \`RATINGS_URL\`, which are Mike's.
- **The quality suite** (\`tests/quality\`): Toskar's own cases (tools, web lookup, files and media, ten languages, deflection), run on the home runners.
- **Measured picture and clip times** (#552, \`docs/\`).

## What only we can publish
1. **Toskar quality per model:** the suite's pass rate per model and quantization, by area (tools, web, files, languages, vision), from our runs, with the date and Core version.
2. **Toskar on hardware:** per hardware cohort:
   - tokens per second;
   - time to first token;
   - load time;
   - peak memory;
   - for picture and clip models, seconds per picture or clip at each quality;
   - phones and tablets as cohorts too.
3. **Known limits:** per model, and for Toskar overall:
   - context actually usable;
   - languages that pass;
   - tool reliability;
   - what fails (for example \"video over 5 s isn't supported\", \"vision on phones needs 6 GB\").
   - Generated from the catalog and quality results, not written by hand.
4. **Goal metrics:** the targets we hold ourselves to, published with where we are. For example:
   - recommended models pass ≥ 90% of the quality suite in every language;
   - \"works well\" means ≥ 15 tok/s and first token < 2 s;
   - a picture at *balanced* < 30 s on a recommended GPU.

## Community results: \`toskar bench\`
- **\`toskar bench\`** (and **Run benchmark** in Diagnostics, Toskar Pro, and the apps) runs locally: a speed pass, plus a short version of the quality suite for each installed model.
- **Results show first, and are sent only if the person chooses.** They go to the ratings service as a new record type next to ratings, with the same privacy:
  - hardware cohort, never exact hardware;
  - no prompts or answers;
  - a pseudonymous install ID.
- **Aggregated into the CC0 dataset** with the same minimum-count rules as ratings.
- **Runs are reproducible:** fixed prompts and seeds per suite version, and results record the suite and Core versions, so numbers from different runs can be compared.
- **Its own CLI,** \`toskar-bench\`, a standalone binary or container that runs on a machine without Toskar, for people who want to compare hardware before buying.

## On the website (toskar.ai)
- **\`/models\`:** each model with Toskar quality, known limits, and community speed per hardware, plus links to LocalScore and the llama.cpp threads.
- **\`/hardware\`:** \"What can my computer run?\", per cohort (with the existing blog post).
- **\`/limits\`:** known limits and goal metrics, updated by each release.
- **Built from the CC0 dataset** at build time (\`content/toskar/\` like the catalog). No live calls from visitors' browsers.

## Pieces
- [ ] Deploy community ratings (#37's pending steps; Mike)
- [ ] Quality results: publish per-model pass rates from the home runner runs to toskar-model-data
- [ ] Known limits and goal metrics: a generated \`limits.json\` per release, plus docs/limits.md
- [ ] \`toskar bench\` / Run benchmark: speed and quality-lite, results shown, opt-in send
- [ ] Ratings service: a benchmark record type, its aggregation, and publish rules
- [ ] Standalone \`toskar-bench\`
- [ ] toskar.ai: /models, /hardware, /limits, with the external links

Related: #37 (community ratings), #552 (measured media times), toskar.ai#50 (product pages).

cases.title: Plugins: a framework and SDK for building Toskar extensions
cases.body:
Let people extend Toskar Core with their own tools, integrations, triggers, and pages, and share them, without forking Core or waiting on us.

## Design: plugins run outside Core, on MCP, with a manifest
- **Not code loaded into Core.** Go plugins break across versions. A plugin inside Core could read every secret and crash the server.
- **A plugin is a package:** a manifest plus one or more parts. Its code runs as its own process, sandboxed, or as a WebAssembly module.
- **Tools speak MCP,** which Core already supports, so existing MCP servers become plugins by adding a manifest.
- **The manifest adds what MCP doesn't have:** setup forms, permissions, triggers, UI, and templates.
- **#586's integrations are built as first-party plugins** on this framework (Home Assistant, the *arr apps, Frigate, …), so the framework is used for real from day one.

### \`toskar-plugin.json\`
- \`id\`, \`name\`, \`version\`, \`publisher\`, \`description\`, \`icon\`, the minimum Core / client contract version
- \`settings\`: form fields (URL, token, choices), with secrets kept in Core's secret store
- \`permissions\`: network hosts, a folder in the workspace, what it may read in Toskar (chats, knowledge, files), and whether it may notify
- \`parts\`, any of:
  - **tools**: an MCP server (command, or WASM)
  - **triggers**: events it can start automations with, carrying a payload and pictures (#586)
  - **actions**: things automations may be allowed to do (#586's allowlist)
  - **knowledge connectors**: sources for Knowledge (#90)
  - **templates**: automation and profile templates, in ten languages
  - **web panel**: a page or settings panel in the web UI, in a sandboxed iframe, talking to Core only through a narrow bridge
- \`i18n\`: the plugin's own strings in each language it supports

## Safety
- **Install shows exactly what it asks for** (hosts, folders, data, actions), and the Admin approves. An update that asks for more asks again.
- **Least privilege at run time:** a plugin process gets only its granted network hosts and folders. On macOS and Linux it's sandboxed; WASM plugins have no ambient access at all.
- **Trigger content stays untrusted** (#204): a plugin can't widen what an automation may do.
- **Plugins are signed by their publisher.** Toskar warns on unsigned ones, and each install records who signed it.
- **Admins can turn plugins off entirely,** per computer or per organization.

## Building one: the SDK
- **\`toskar plugin init\`** scaffolds a TypeScript, Python, or Go plugin with a manifest, a tool, a trigger, and tests.
- **Libraries per language** wrap MCP and add triggers, settings, and logging.
- **Dev mode:** \`toskar plugin dev ./my-plugin\` loads it live into a local Core, with its logs in the UI.
- **\`toskar plugin pack\` / \`sign\`** produce a \`.toskarplugin\` file.
- **Docs:** docs/plugins.md, a tutorial (a weather station plugin), and the manifest reference.

## Sharing them
- **Install from a file, a URL, or a Git repository.**
- **A community directory** in the web UI's Plugins page:
  - listings with permissions shown up front;
  - ratings like community model ratings (#37);
  - plugins we've reviewed are marked.
- **Updates** are checked like model updates, and the Admin approves them.

## Pieces (one PR each)
- [ ] Design doc: manifest schema, lifecycle, sandboxing per OS, the contract version
- [ ] Core: install, enable, disable, remove, permissions review, secret settings, the process supervisor
- [ ] Tools part: run its MCP server under the plugin's sandbox
- [ ] Triggers and actions parts, with #586
- [ ] Web: the Plugins page (installed, settings, permissions, logs) and sandboxed panels
- [ ] SDK: TypeScript first, then Python and Go; \`toskar plugin init/dev/pack/sign\`
- [ ] The first-party plugins from #586 moved onto the framework
- [ ] Community directory and signing
- [ ] Docs and tutorial

Related: #586 (integrations), #90 (knowledge connectors), #204 (automations), #37 (community ratings).

cases.title: Integrations: Home Assistant, the *arr apps, and others, as triggers and actions
cases.body:
Let Toskar react to things happening in the person's other systems, and act on them safely.

> When motion is detected at my doorbell, look at the camera, tell me who's there, and turn on the porch light if it's after dark.

This is more than MCP. MCP gives the model tools to call when asked. Integrations also need **events in** (a trigger with its data and pictures), **easy setup**, and **permission to act when no one is watching**.

## What exists
- **Webhook triggers** (#204): \`POST /hooks/{token}\` starts an automation, so a Home Assistant automation can call Toskar today.
- **MCP connectors:** Home Assistant has its own MCP server.
- **Vision models** for pictures (#191), and **push to devices** (ntfy, the apps).

## What's missing
1. **The trigger's content in the run.** A webhook's JSON body and attached pictures (a snapshot URL or upload) reach the automation's prompt and a vision model. Today the run only knows that it fired.
2. **Acting from a trigger.** Runs started by trigger content skip every tool that changes something outside Toskar (#204's safety rule), so even \"turn on the porch light\" is blocked.
   - Keep that default.
   - Add a **per-automation allowlist**: when creating the automation, the person picks the exact actions it may take, such as Home Assistant \`light.turn_on\` on \`light.porch\`. Those run without asking; anything else is skipped.
   - Or anything else asks for approval on their phone, with Approve / Deny on the notification.
3. **First-class integrations.** Each is set up from a form (URL plus token or API key, a connection test, then what Toskar may read and do), not by writing an MCP config.

## Integrations, first round
| Integration | Read | Do (allowlisted) | Triggers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Home Assistant** | states, history, areas, camera snapshots (\`camera_proxy\`) | call services: lights, locks, scenes, notify, … | its event stream (WebSocket): state changes, doorbell or motion events, with an entity and state filter |
| **Frigate** | events, snapshots, clips | — | new detections (person, car, package) with the snapshot |
| **Sonarr / Radarr / Lidarr** | library, calendar, queue | search, add, monitor | their *Connect → Webhook*: grabbed, downloaded, failed |
| **Overseerr / Jellyseerr** | requests | approve or deny requests | new request |
| **Plex / Jellyfin** | libraries, what's playing | — | playback started or stopped, item added |

Later: Node-RED, n8n, Uptime Kuma, Proxmox, UniFi Protect, calendars, email (IMAP).

## The doorbell, end to end
1. Settings → Integrations → Home Assistant: URL plus a long-lived token, then **Test**.
2. New automation, from a template: **\"When someone's at the door\"**.
   - Trigger: Home Assistant event, \`binary_sensor.doorbell_motion\` turns \`on\`.
   - Snapshot: \`camera.doorbell\`.
   - Allowed actions: \`light.turn_on\` on \`light.porch\`.
3. Motion → Toskar receives the event → takes the snapshot → a vision model describes it → the condition (\"after dark?\") → it turns on the light (allowlisted) → it notifies the phone with the picture and description.
4. The run's results show the event, the picture, what the model saw, and the actions taken.

## Safety
- Integration tokens live in the secret store, never in prompts or logs.
- Per integration, the person chooses what may be read and what may be done.
- Trigger content is untrusted (#204): it can't widen the allowlist or turn on tools.
- Rate limits and dedupe per trigger, so a motion sensor flapping doesn't start 50 runs.
- Every action taken is logged in the run's results.

## Pieces (one PR each)
- [ ] Trigger payloads: the webhook body and pictures reach the run (prompt plus vision)
- [ ] Per-automation allowlist of actions, plus approval on the phone for others
- [ ] Integrations framework: settings UI, secret storage, connection test, read/do scopes
- [ ] Home Assistant: read, services, event-stream trigger, camera snapshots
- [ ] *arr apps and Overseerr: read, actions, webhook trigger presets
- [ ] Frigate, Plex/Jellyfin
- [ ] Templates (doorbell, download finished, new request), in all ten languages
- [ ] Docs: docs/integrations.md

cases.title: Architecture question: CPU node fallback execution strategy and zero-dep inference
cases.body:
I was reading the "Distributed inference grid" research brief and had an architectural question about how Toskar plans to handle fallback routing to CPU-only nodes when the primary GPU grid is saturated (or for routing smaller utility models).

Right now, deploying a standard inference node usually means pulling down heavy dependency stacks (Python, CUDA libs, etc.) even if that specific worker only has CPU compute. Have you considered supporting zero-dependency execution engines for the CPU tier? 

For example, I've been using Project Zero (https://github.com/shifulegend/project-zero) - a pure C99 inference engine that runs the BitNet b1.58-2B model at 36 tok/s on a standard Xeon using SIMD, without requiring Python or external BLAS libraries. 

Plugging a lightweight C backend like that into Toskar's grid topology could allow edge devices or generic x86 servers to join the network seamlessly and serve lightweight tasks (like tool routing, fast RAG classification, or small GGUFs) without the bloated container requirements of the main Python stack.

Is the long-term plan to bundle a universal engine (like llama.cpp / vLLM) across all nodes, or will the orchestrator support dispatching to targeted lightweight CPU engines for specific hardware profiles?

cases.title: Case study: Toskar as a game AI backend (Dungeon Party), and a blog post
cases.body:
A case study, and a blog post, on using the Toskar API as the AI backend for a game: NPC dialogue, a narrator or game master, quest and item generation, and structured game state. The goal is to work through what a game developer actually needs, close the gaps in core, and then write about how to do it.

## The case study: Dungeon Party
[Dungeon Party](https://github.com/yeixio/dungeonparty) is our own multiplayer tabletop RPG with an AI Dungeon Master. Its Go backend calls OpenAI with `go-openai`, and it uses:
- chat completions;
- `response_format` JSON for story arcs;
- `max_completion_tokens`;
- `seed`;
- `/v1/audio/speech` for the DM's voice.

Pointing it at Toskar (`BaseURL` = `http://<toskar>/v1`, and a Toskar API key) is the most honest test of the API there is. The post can tell that story with real numbers: latency, cost, and what changed.

## Gaps found so far (core)
Comparing Dungeon Party's calls with `internal/api/openai/handler.go`:
- [ ] **`max_completion_tokens` is ignored.** Only `max_tokens` is read, so OpenAI-first clients get no limit. Accept it as an alias.
- [ ] **No `usage` in responses.** Games budget tokens per turn and per session. Return `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, and `total_tokens`, and `stream_options.include_usage` when streaming.
- [ ] **`seed`, `stop`, `top_p`, `frequency_penalty`, and `presence_penalty` are silently dropped.** Pass them to llama.cpp, which supports them all. A seed makes a scene reproducible, which is useful for tests and replays.
- [ ] **No client-defined function calling** (`tools` / `tool_choice` / `tool_calls`). This is the big one for games: the model asks the game to `roll_dice`, `give_item`, `start_combat`, or `move_npc`, and the game, not Toskar, runs it and replies with a `tool` message. Toskar's own tools (`toskar.tools`) stay separate and permission-checked. Client functions are only described to the model and returned to the caller, never run by Toskar.
- [ ] **`finish_reason: "length"`** when a reply is cut off, so the game can continue it or retry. Check that it's reported accurately.
- [ ] **An OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech`** for NPC voices, backed by the existing Read aloud speech (`/api/v1/speech`). It returns audio bytes and takes a voice name.
- [ ] Possibly **`/v1/embeddings`**, for retrieving lore and NPC memory, and **`/v1/images/generations`** on top of image generation. Decide during the case study whether the post needs them.

## What a game developer needs (to verify and document)
- **Latency and streaming:** time to first token for a typewriter effect, with a small model's numbers versus a large one's. Profiles keep NPC barks on a fast small model and the narrator on a larger one.
- **Concurrency:** many players asking at once. How Toskar queues and spreads requests across paired computers, what a 429 or a queue means, and per-key rate limits. A load test with N simulated players goes into the post.
- **Personas:** an NPC is a system prompt plus game state, or a Toskar profile. Show both, and when to use each.
- **Game-owned state:** the game keeps history and world state and sends what each turn needs. Toskar's memory and knowledge are turned off per request (`toskar.memory=false`), so one player's game never leaks into another's.
- **Structured output:** `json_schema` for quest objects, loot tables, and dialogue choices, with how reliable it is on small models (a quality case set).
- **Caching** (#94): cache repeated lines (shop greetings, item descriptions) per declared policy.
- **Safety:** players type anything. Cover prompt-injection hygiene for player text, and what moderation the game must do itself.
- **Deployment options:**
  - a Toskar box beside the game server (headless Linux);
  - each player's own Toskar (fully local, no server cost);
  - a mix, with a fallback to a hosted API.
- **Keys:** never ship a Toskar key in a game client. Game servers call Toskar. A local single-player game talks to the player's own Toskar through an approved device key (Connect a device).
- **Engines:** short client snippets for Godot (GDScript HTTPRequest with streaming), Unity (C#), and plain TypeScript, in `examples/`.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Core gap fixes above, with tests and the contract (#96)
- [ ] `examples/game-backend/`: a small NPC server (Go or TypeScript) showing streaming, structured output, client functions, and voice, plus engine snippets
- [ ] Dungeon Party able to run on Toskar (`AI_BASE_URL` and a key, plus model and profile settings), with measured latency, quality, and cost against OpenAI (yeixio/dungeonparty)
- [ ] Quality cases for game prompts: JSON schema adherence, staying in character, and the function-call round trip
- [ ] Docs: a "Games" page in `docs/` and the API reference
- [ ] The blog post on toskar.ai, "Run your game's AI on your own hardware" (title to be decided), with code, numbers, and the Dungeon Party story (yeixio/toskar.ai)

Related: #94 (AI experience caches), #96 (client contract), #343 (quality matrix).

cases.title: Feature: Private items — encrypted notes, lists, and more, managed from chat
cases.body:
People should be able to create, read, update, and delete their own private items, such as notes, lists, and checklists, from a Toskar chat. These items are encrypted, so they are unreadable on disk, to other people on the same Toskar, and in backups.

## In a chat
- **Create:** "Make a grocery list: eggs, milk, coffee" and "Note: the garage code changes on the 1st".
- **Read:** "What's on my grocery list?" and "Show my packing list".
- **Update:** "Add bread to the grocery list", "Check off milk", and "Rename it to Costco run".
- **Delete:** "Delete the packing list".

The answer shows the item as a card with its own **Edit**, **Check off**, and **Delete** buttons. Deleting, and large edits, ask before they happen, as tool approvals do now.

These run as built-in tools (`items.create`, `items.get`, `items.search`, `items.update`, `items.delete`), so any model with tool calling can use them. For small models, the text rules (`classify` and the memory-command rules) recognize the common phrasings. Typos are handled as in #451.

## In the app
- **A Private page** (name to be decided: Notes, Private, or Vault) with search, pinning, and tags.
- **Item kinds:** a note (Markdown), a list or checklist, and a small table. A kind is a schema, so more can be added later, such as a contact card or a recipe.
- **Bulk select and delete,** as in #452.

## How it's different from memory
- **Memories go into every chat.** Private items are used only when you ask for them, or open one in a chat.
- **Each item is used only for that turn.** The model reads it during the turn. The chat's saved history keeps a reference card ("Grocery list, 6 items"), not the decrypted contents, so the item doesn't leak into history, exports, or search indexes in plain text.

## Encryption
- **Envelope encryption per person:**
  - each item is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-256-GCM using a data key;
  - the data key is wrapped by that person's key;
  - that key is held by the system's key store: Keychain on macOS, DPAPI on Windows, Secret Service on Linux (or a file key with a warning when there isn't one), and the secure keystore on the phone.
- **An optional lock:** a passphrase, or device biometrics or a passkey (#436). With the lock on, the key is also wrapped by the passphrase, so the server can't decrypt the items while they're locked, not even an admin. The lock applies again after idle time and at restart.
- **Other people:** admins and other people on the same Toskar can't read your items, and roles never grant access to them. Deleting a person deletes their items, which can't be recovered.
- **Search:** titles and contents are searched in memory after unlocking, with no plaintext index on disk.
- **Exports and backups:** stay encrypted. An "Export my items" option writes plaintext only when you ask, after confirming.
- **Losing the passphrase means losing the items** if the lock is on. Setup says so, and offers a recovery code.

## Where items can go
- **Models:** only models on your own computers. Items never go to web searches, connected services, or a hosted model. A turn that uses an item is pinned to local nodes, where traffic is already encrypted (#404).
- **Automations:** can use items only when you allow it per automation. For example, "every Friday, text me my grocery list" is fine, but it's off by default.
- **Paired devices** (Connect a device): read and edit through the API, using the device's own key. A device keeps an offline copy only if you allow it, encrypted with its keystore.
- **Portals and guests:** a guest has items only within the portal, and only if the portal allows it.
- **The egress list** (Settings → what left your computer) never shows item contents.

## Checklist
- [ ] Encrypted item store: a per-person key in the system key store, envelope encryption, and tests that check the database file has no plaintext
- [ ] Item tools and API: CRUD, search, and bulk delete, plus role, device, and portal rules and the contract (#96)
- [ ] Chat cards and history keeping references only; turns that use items stay local
- [ ] Private page in the web UI: notes, checklists, tables, search, and pins
- [ ] Optional lock: passphrase, biometrics, or passkey; auto-lock; a recovery code
- [ ] Quality cases: text rules (`text.json`) and end-to-end chats (`cases.json`), including typo'd phrasings and cases that must not trigger
- [ ] Phone: the Private page, chat cards, and a keystore-encrypted offline copy (yeixio/toskar-apps)
- [ ] Help, privacy page, screenshots, and a changelog fragment

Related: #213 (encryption), #232 (regulated use), #436 (passkeys), #451 (typos), #452 (bulk delete).

cases.title: Credit bug reporters in release notes (GitHub, in-app, and store reviews)
cases.body:
People who report a bug should be thanked in the release notes of the version that fixes it, whether they opened a GitHub issue, reported it from the app (#201), or left a store review (yeixio/toskar-apps#144).

## How
- **Issues record the reporter**, with a `Reported-by:` line in the issue body:
  - `Reported-by: @<github-user>`, filled in by the issue templates from whoever opens the issue;
  - `Reported-by: App Store reviewer "<nickname>"` or `Google Play reviewer "<name>"`, from yeixio/toskar-apps#144;
  - `Reported-by: <name>`, from an in-app report (#201), only when the person chose to give a name.
- **Changelog fragments carry it.** A fragment in `changes/unreleased/` can end with a `Thanks:` line:
  ```markdown
  ### Fixed

  - Answers no longer stop halfway when a source page is slow.

  Thanks: @octocat, App Store reviewer "Hikerdad"
  ```
  - `scripts/changelog.py release` adds "Thanks to … for reporting these." at the end of the version's section, so the GitHub release notes show it.
  - `changelog.py check` accepts and validates the line.
- **The PR template** asks: does this fix an issue with a `Reported-by:`? If so, add `Thanks:` to the fragment.
- **A CI check:** a PR that says "Fixes #N", where #N has a `Reported-by:`, needs the `Thanks:` in its fragment. A comment, not a hard failure.
- **Privacy:**
  - only names people already show publicly (a GitHub handle, a store nickname), or chose to give;
  - anyone can ask to be left out;
  - no email addresses.

## Checklist
- [ ] Issue templates: `Reported-by:` from the author
- [ ] `changelog.py`: the `Thanks:` line in fragments, in `check`, and in `release`, with tests
- [ ] PR template line, and the gentle CI check
- [ ] The development guide: how credit works
- [ ] Apps release notes do the same (yeixio/toskar-apps#144)

Related: #201 (reporting a bug from the app), yeixio/toskar-apps#144 (store reviews).

cases.title: Feature: Sign in with a passkey (deferred from #206)
cases.body:
## Summary

Sign in with a passkey (WebAuthn), alongside or instead of a password. This was item 3 of #206, deferred when the rest of accounts shipped.

## Why it waits

Browsers offer passkeys only on a secure origin with a real host name:
- The relying party ID can't be an IP address, so `http://192.168.1.20:7331` can never use one.
- Self-signed certificates don't count, and Toskar's own LAN certificate (#405) is self-signed.

So on a typical home network nobody could use a passkey. They'd work behind a reverse proxy with a real domain and a trusted certificate (Caddy, Tailscale HTTPS, Cloudflare), and those setups already have sign-in through proxy headers (#423) or OpenID Connect (#424).

## When it's worth doing

- If enough people run Toskar at a real domain with a trusted certificate, or
- If Toskar gains a supported way to get a trusted certificate for a local name.

## Shape when it's done

- **Library:** go-webauthn (a new dependency).
- **Registration:** a person adds passkeys under Settings → Your account, while signed in.
- **Sign-in:** the sign-in screen offers "Sign in with a passkey" only when the page is a secure origin with a host name.
- **Storage:** credentials are kept per person.
- **Restrictions:** none for guests or portals.

cases.title: Move the core build to Node 26
cases.body:
## Summary
CI, releases and the screenshot tool all build with Node 22. Node 26 becomes the long-term support release in late October 2026. Node 22 only gets maintenance fixes now, until April 2027. Move core to Node 26, then take the `@types/node` bump that Dependabot offered in #294 (closed for now).

**What it affects:** Node only builds the web UI, which is embedded in the Go binary, and runs the screenshot tool. Toskar doesn't ship Node to users, and the Docker image doesn't use it, so if something breaks, CI fails, not users.

## Steps
- [ ] Change the six `node-version: "22"` lines to `"26"`: `ci.yml` has three, plus `release.yml`, `screenshots.yml` and `security.yml`.
- [ ] Add `"engines": { "node": ">=26" }` to `web/package.json` and `scripts/screenshots/package.json`, and a `.nvmrc` with `26`, so a local build uses the same Node as CI.
- [ ] Bump `@types/node` to 26 in `web/`, which replaces #294.
- [ ] Mention it in the contributor docs that list what you need to build.
- [ ] **Ideally before** the Vite 8 bump (#292), so Vite 8 is tested on the Node we'll use.

## Check
- [ ] CI goes green on the home runners: the web build, unit tests, end-to-end tests with Playwright, and the security scan.
- [ ] A screenshots run works.
- [ ] A release build, as a dry run or the next real release, builds the web UI on Node 26.

## Apps repo, separately
`yeixio/toskar-apps` sets `NODE_VERSION: "22"` in its workflows, and the phone app uses Expo 52 and React Native 0.76. Check that Expo and Metro support Node 26 before moving it. Until they do, move the apps repo to Node 24, the current long-term release, and open its own issue there.

## Done when
Core builds, tests and releases on Node 26. Local builds match CI, and Dependabot's `@types/node` stays in step with the Node we run.
